nodes.label: Option<T>
nodes.rationale: Some<T> | None - preferred over T | null in domain-API returns and long-lived fields because the type forces the empty case to be handled at the point of use rather than remembered. Nullable stays right in three places the framework uses it deliberately: hot-path internal fields where the wrapper would show in a profile, serialization boundaries that round-trip through null, and optional parameters with ergonomic defaults.

nodes.label: Try<T>
nodes.rationale: Success<T> | Failure - turns a throw into a value you can pass around, which is what you want when the failure has to travel into a message, across an ask, or into a state machine.

nodes.label: Either<L, R>
nodes.rationale: Left | Right, right-biased. Reach for it over Try when the failure side is a domain value you want typed - a validation report, a rejection reason - rather than a thrown error.

nodes.label: Lazy<T>
nodes.rationale: Scala's lazy val: the computation runs on first get() and the result is memoised, including a thrown failure, so expensive or side-effecting setup happens exactly once however many callers ask. reset() and setOverride() exist for tests - they are why a lazily-imported backend can be swapped for a fake without touching the production path.

nodes.label: RingBuffer<T>
nodes.rationale: A FIFO queue whose removal from the front is O(1). It exists because Array.prototype.shift() reindexes every element still queued, so taking one item costs more the deeper the queue - invisible at ten, expensive at a hundred thousand, which is what a mailbox becomes when it falls behind its producers. Four operations and nothing else, deliberately: every extra operation is another index-wrapping edge case in a type on the message path of every actor. drain() releases the backing store so a queue that grew to a million gives the memory back.

nodes.label: BidirectionalMap<K, V>
nodes.rationale: A Map that also answers value -> key. It exists because a hand-written reverse index is two maps that must be updated in lockstep, and the failure mode when they drift is silent. set() displaces rather than throwing - the one departure from the Map contract it implements, deliberate so the type stays usable wherever a Map is expected; trySet reports the collision instead.

nodes.label: BidirectionalMultiMap<L, R>
nodes.rationale: Many lefts to many rights, answering in both directions - the shape a subscription registry has, where the message telling you a subscriber is gone carries only the subscriber. The invariant: there is no such thing as an empty participant, since one would be invisible to a pair count while still occupying a topic cap. get() hands back the LIVE set rather than a copy, a deliberate trade because the relation is read once per published message on fan-out paths where an O(n) copy per read is not payable.

nodes.label: SameValueZero equality in both bidirectional types
nodes.rationale: Both directions are backed by Map and Set, so NaN works as a key, 0 and -0 are the same, and two structurally equal objects are two different values. When you need structural identity, index a derived string - which is what the framework does, keying on ref.path.toString() rather than on the ref, because a Terminated carries the cell's own self ref rather than the object that subscribed.

nodes.label: randomString / randomHex / randomId / randomUuid
nodes.rationale: The first three draw from globalThis.crypto and correct the modulo bias a plain byte % alphabet.length introduces. randomId is the one for naming an actor, because an actor name ends up in a path and a path is an address - a counter makes that address guessable, which is why anonymous actors and ask reply refs are named from here. randomHex exists separately because W3C trace-context mandates its alphabet. randomUuid's 122 random bits are what it takes to stay distinct from an id minted in another process years later.

nodes.label: ExistsPredicate
nodes.source_location: ### Drawing until you get a free one
nodes.rationale: The optional collision check all four random helpers take, where true means 'taken, draw again'. It is named exists and inverted that way because the callback IS the while condition of the do/while loop it replaces - an accept-predicate would read as that loop's negation and put a ! on every Map- or Set-backed call site. After 1000 draws it throws rather than looping forever, because a call that never returns is the worse failure.

nodes.label: safeStringify(value, maxLength?)
nodes.source_location: ## Stringifying a value that already went wrong
nodes.rationale: Renders any value as a string and never throws. JSON.stringify throws on a circular structure and on a BigInt, so using it to build a log line risks replacing the problem you were reporting with one thrown from inside the reporting code - exactly the situation an onReceive logging an unexpected message is in. Lossy on purpose: the output is for a human, not a parser, and is capped at 8 KiB so it cannot grow into a multi-megabyte string that blocks the event loop.

nodes.label: redactUrlCredentials(value)
nodes.source_location: ## Logging a URL without logging the password
nodes.rationale: Masks the userinfo and changes nothing else - no normalisation, no trailing slash, no lowercased host - so an operator still recognises the value they typed. A strict no-op on anything without a scheme://...@ authority, which makes it safe to apply unconditionally to a value that only might be a URL.

nodes.label: redactedUrlLabel(value)
nodes.source_location: ## Logging a URL without logging the password
nodes.rationale: Reduces a URL to a stable identity - scheme, host, port, path - dropping userinfo AND the query string, because a WebSocket endpoint is commonly authenticated with a ?token=. The path is kept deliberately since it is what tells two connections to the same host apart; use it for a line emitted repeatedly.

nodes.label: lazyImportModule(name, options?)
nodes.rationale: Imports a module dynamically and, when missing, throws an error naming the package and the install command. The pattern every broker, cache and persistence backend is built on: the module must not be a hard dependency, so the import has to be dynamic, so the default failure is a bare 'Cannot find module' that says nothing useful. Normalising a default export is deliberately left to the caller, since the right unwrapping differs per module.

nodes.label: OptionsBuilder
nodes.rationale: A builder IS its settings: the protected set writes each field as an own enumerable property, so an instance is structurally a bag of the fields you set and a plain object is interchangeable with it.

nodes.label: OptionsValidator
nodes.rationale: Check helpers take only the field name, which is typo-checked against the options type and a compile error on a field of the wrong type. Every helper is a no-op when the field is undefined, so an unset optional always passes and required-ness stays wherever you enforce it; a rejected value throws OptionsError, with a URL's credentials masked.
